# ===== CELL 3 =====
class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, rnn_type='RNN', input_size=28,
                 hidden_size=128, num_layers=1, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.rnn_type = rnn_type

        if rnn_type == 'RNN':
            self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size,
                              num_layers, batch_first=True)
        elif rnn_type == 'LSTM':
            self.rnn = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size,
                               num_layers, batch_first=True)
        elif rnn_type == 'GRU':
            self.rnn = nn.GRU(input_size, hidden_size,
                              num_layers, batch_first=True)
        else:
            raise ValueError(rnn_type)

        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: [batch, time_step, input_size]
        if self.rnn_type == 'LSTM':
            r_out, (h_n, c_n) = self.rnn(x, None)
        else:
            r_out, h_n = self.rnn(x, None)

        out = self.out(r_out[:, -1, :])
        return out

model = Net(rnn_type='RNN', hidden_size=128)
if cuda:
    model.cuda()

optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
print(model)

def train_epoch(model, optimizer, epoch, tag):
    model.train()
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    running_loss = 0.0
    correct = 0
    total = 0

    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
        if cuda:
            data, target = data.cuda(), target.cuda()

        data = data.view(-1, 28, 28)   # [B, 1, 28, 28] -> [B, 28, 28]

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(data)
        loss = criterion(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        running_loss += loss.item()
        correct += (output.argmax(1) == target).sum().item()
        total += target.size(0)

        if batch_idx % logging_interval == 0:
            print(f'{tag} Train Epoch {epoch} '
                  f'[{batch_idx * len(data)}/{len(train_loader.dataset)}] '
                  f'Loss: {loss.item():.6f}')

    train_loss = running_loss / len(train_loader)
    train_acc = correct / total
    writer.add_scalar(f'{tag}/Loss/train', train_loss, epoch)
    writer.add_scalar(f'{tag}/Accuracy/train', train_acc, epoch)
    print(f"{tag} epoch {epoch}: train_loss={train_loss:.4f}, "
          f"train_acc={train_acc:.4f}")
    return train_loss, train_acc


def test_epoch(model, epoch, tag):
    model.eval()
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    test_loss = 0.0
    correct = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for data, target in test_loader:
            if cuda:
                data, target = data.cuda(), target.cuda()
            data = data.view(-1, 28, 28)

            output = model(data)
            test_loss += criterion(output, target).item()
            correct += (output.argmax(1) == target).sum().item()

    test_loss /= len(test_loader)
    test_acc = correct / len(test_loader.dataset)
    writer.add_scalar(f'{tag}/Loss/test', test_loss, epoch)
    writer.add_scalar(f'{tag}/Accuracy/test', test_acc, epoch)
    print(f"{tag} test epoch {epoch}: loss={test_loss:.4f}, "
          f"acc={100 * test_acc:.2f}%\n")
    return test_loss, test_acc

3(a) Baseline RNN — observations¶

With hidden size 128, Adam at lr = 0.01 and 10 epochs, the plain RNN is highly unstable. Test accuracy per epoch is 53.90%, 30.80%, 46.07%, 38.65%, 41.56%, 23.03%, 31.91%, 45.69%, 26.50%, 30.06%. The best test accuracy is 53.90% at epoch 1, and the final test accuracy is 30.06% at epoch 10. Train loss oscillates in the 1.3283–1.9365 band (mean ≈ 1.6489). Train accuracy ranges from 29.62% to 53.13% and ends at 35.12%. This instability is consistent with vanishing / exploding gradients across the 28 recurrent time steps.

In [6]:
def run_mnist_experiment(rnn_type='RNN', hidden_size=128,
                         n_epochs=5, lr=0.01):
    m = Net(rnn_type=rnn_type, hidden_size=hidden_size)
    if cuda:
        m.cuda()
    opt = optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr)
    tag = f'{rnn_type}_h{hidden_size}'

    hist = {'train_loss': [], 'train_acc': [],
            'test_loss': [], 'test_acc': []}

    for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
        tr_loss, tr_acc = train_epoch(m, opt, epoch, tag)
        te_loss, te_acc = test_epoch(m, epoch, tag)
        hist['train_loss'].append(tr_loss)
        hist['train_acc'].append(tr_acc)
        hist['test_loss'].append(te_loss)
        hist['test_acc'].append(te_acc)

    return hist

]

all_hist = {}
for rnn_type, hidden_size in experiments:
    tag = f'{rnn_type}_h{hidden_size}'
    print(f"\n===== Running {tag} =====")
    all_hist[tag] = run_mnist_experiment(
        rnn_type=rnn_type,
        hidden_size=hidden_size,
        n_epochs=SEARCH_EPOCHS,
        lr=lr
    )

print("\nFinal test accuracies:")
for tag, hist in all_hist.items():
    print(tag, hist['test_acc'][-1])

3(b) RNN vs. LSTM vs. GRU — observations¶

All results below use Adam, lr = 0.01, and 5 epochs. To avoid mixing separate runs, the hidden-size table uses Cell 7 for the plain RNN and the dedicated sweeps in Cell 10 (LSTM) and Cell 11 (GRU). Cell 7 also contains exploratory LSTM_h128 and GRU_h128 runs that reached 92.74% and 89.04% respectively; those are different runs and are not used in the hidden-size table. The authoritative LSTM_h128 result is 94.26% from Cell 10, and the authoritative GRU_h128 result is 92.04% from Cell 11.

Plain RNN hidden-size sweep (Cell 7).

  • h = 64: final train/test loss 1.3745 / 1.4455, test accuracy 45.07%
  • h = 128: final train/test loss 1.5071 / 1.4192, test accuracy 46.41%
  • h = 256: final train/test loss 2.4683 / 2.4925, test accuracy 9.58%

The plain RNN gets worse as width increases at lr = 0.01. The h = 256 run essentially collapses to chance. This is an optimisation / gradient-stability problem, not a capacity limit: the same h = 256 RNN trained at lr = 1e-3 reaches 95.67% by epoch 5 in the optional Cell 9 run.

LSTM hidden-size sweep (Cell 10).

  • h = 64: final train/test loss 0.1452 / 0.1479, test accuracy 95.63%
  • h = 128: final train/test loss 0.1752 / 0.1931, test accuracy 94.26%
  • h = 256: final train/test loss 0.3534 / 0.2233, test accuracy 93.26%

All three LSTM sizes are above 93%. Accuracy decreases monotonically as width increases in this run: 95.63% → 94.26% → 93.26%. Loss is also lowest at h = 64: both final train loss and final test loss are smallest at h = 64.

GRU hidden-size sweep (Cell 11).

  • h = 64: final train/test loss 0.2228 / 0.2120, test accuracy 93.77%
  • h = 128: final train/test loss 0.2955 / 0.2566, test accuracy 92.04%
  • h = 256: final train/test loss 0.2854 / 0.3507, test accuracy 89.22%

The GRU is less sensitive to width than the plain RNN, but in this rerun its accuracy also decreases monotonically with width: 93.77% → 92.04% → 89.22%. The spread is about 4.55 percentage points. h = 64 gives the best test accuracy and the lowest test loss; h = 256 gives the worst test accuracy and the highest test loss.

Comparison at h = 128 using the dedicated sweeps. RNN h = 128: 46.41%; LSTM h = 128: 94.26%; GRU h = 128: 92.04%. Both gated models clearly beat the plain RNN: the LSTM is +47.85 pp above the RNN and the GRU is +45.63 pp above the RNN. The LSTM is slightly ahead of the GRU by 2.22 pp at this width.

Are LSTM / GRU better? Yes. The plain RNN is unstable at lr = 0.01, while both gated variants converge to >89% test accuracy. Best overall results in the sweeps: LSTM h = 64 → 95.63%, LSTM h = 128 → 94.26%, GRU h = 64 → 93.77%, LSTM h = 256 → 93.26%, GRU h = 128 → 92.04%, GRU h = 256 → 89.22%.

GRU / LSTM loss plots. The two dedicated figures are produced in Cell 12:

  1. LSTM vs. GRU train/test loss at h = 128.
  2. RNN vs. LSTM vs. GRU train/test loss at h = 128.

These are the figures that satisfy the “plots for LSTM/GRU loss” checklist item.

# ===== 3(b) hidden-size sweep for the LSTM =====
lstm_sweep = {}
for h in [64, 128, 256]:
    tag = f'LSTM_h{h}'
    print(f"\n===== Running {tag} =====")
    lstm_sweep[h] = run_mnist_experiment(
        rnn_type='LSTM', hidden_size=h, n_epochs=5, lr=0.01
    )

print("\nLSTM final test accuracy by hidden size:")
for h, hist in lstm_sweep.items():
    print(f"  h={h:>3d}: {hist['test_acc'][-1]:.4f}")

# Plot: test accuracy per epoch for each hidden size
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
for h, hist in lstm_sweep.items():
    plt.plot(hist['test_acc'], marker='o', label=f'LSTM h={h}')
plt.title('LSTM: effect of hidden size on test accuracy (lr=0.01, 5 epochs)')
plt.xlabel('Epoch'); plt.ylabel('Test accuracy')
plt.legend(); plt.grid(True); plt.show()

# Plot: train + test loss per epoch for each hidden size
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
for h, hist in lstm_sweep.items():
    plt.plot(hist['train_loss'], marker='o', label=f'LSTM h={h} train')
    plt.plot(hist['test_loss'],  marker='s', linestyle='--', label=f'LSTM h={h} test')
plt.title('LSTM: effect of hidden size on train & test loss (lr=0.01, 5 epochs)')
plt.xlabel('Epoch'); plt.ylabel('Loss')

3(c) Comparison with the CNN from Assignment 1¶

CNN baseline. In Assignment 1, the best CNN reached 99.30% test accuracy on MNIST (SGD + Momentum run). The LeNet5 result on CIFAR-10 in Problem 1 is not a fair MNIST comparison because it uses a different dataset; the relevant baseline is the Assignment 1 MNIST CNN.

RNN / gated RNN results on MNIST. Using the dedicated Part 3 sweeps:

  • Plain RNN h = 128: 46.41% at 5 epochs.
  • LSTM h = 128: 94.26% at 5 epochs.
  • GRU h = 128: 92.04% at 5 epochs.
  • Best LSTM in the sweep: h = 64, 95.63%.
  • Best GRU in the sweep: h = 64, 93.77%.

The plain RNN is also unstable: the 10-epoch baseline peaks at 53.90% and ends at 30.06%, with large epoch-to-epoch swings in train loss and test accuracy.

Quantitative gap. Using the Assignment 1 CNN accuracy 99.30%:

  • CNN vs. plain RNN h = 128: 99.30 − 46.41 = 52.89 pp.
  • CNN vs. LSTM h = 128: 99.30 − 94.26 = 5.04 pp.
  • CNN vs. GRU h = 128: 99.30 − 92.04 = 7.26 pp.
  • CNN vs. best LSTM h = 64: 99.30 − 95.63 = 3.67 pp.
  • CNN vs. best GRU h = 64: 99.30 − 93.77 = 5.53 pp.

The CNN outperformed the plain RNN by about 52.89 percentage points, and still outperformed the best gated RNN by roughly 3.67–5.53 percentage points. These are percentage-point gaps, not percent gaps.

Why the CNN wins. A CNN encodes 2-D locality, weight sharing, and translation equivariance directly into the architecture. A row-wise RNN treats each 28×28 image as 28 sequential 28-vector inputs, so vertical spatial structure must be learned through 28 recurrent updates. The plain RNN also suffers from vanishing / exploding gradients, which is exactly what the h = 256 collapse to 9.58% at lr = 0.01 demonstrates. LSTM / GRU gates largely fix the gradient problem and recover most of the accuracy, but the recurrent models are still sequential over time steps and do not have the CNN’s 2-D inductive bias.

Similarities. Both are trained end-to-end with cross-entropy, both learn hierarchical features, and both are sensitive to learning rate and input normalisation.

Differences / practical takeaway. CNNs are the right default for static images. RNNs / LSTMs / GRUs are preferable when the data is genuinely sequential, e.g. handwriting strokes, audio, or video frames. Gated RNNs make row-wise MNIST trainable, but even the best gated RNN in this notebook remains below the Assignment 1 CNN.
